## TL;DR

Built a narrow-screen Settings composition for viewports below the shared 720 CSS pixel boundary. Mobile Settings now presents its existing seven destinations in a two-column, touch-sized section chooser, then displays the same panels and configuration controls used by desktop. Desktop retains its current tab strip at 720px and above. The Settings store, schema, URL tab selection, autosave, save status, and save errors remain the source of truth.

## Work and rationale

The implementation follows ADR 0011’s one-SPA, viewport-selected composition. Settings already had stable route-addressable tabs through `SETTINGS_TABS`, `activeTab`, and `setTab`, so the mobile chooser uses that same list and route update function. It does not introduce new categories, duplicate forms, or a second save path. This keeps direct links such as `/settings?tab=notifications` working and preserves existing query handling for General sections.

At narrow widths, the chooser is a two-column panel with explicit active state and a 44px minimum button height. The desktop `role=tablist` remains the desktop navigation and is hidden under the mobile breakpoint; the new navigation uses regular buttons with `aria-current`, keyboard focus styling, and no hover dependency. Existing content panels remain shared, which also means schema-derived fields and hand-built settings such as themes, publishing, attachments, and service settings stay in sync between compositions.

The mobile CSS stacks setting rows, lets labels and values wrap, allows inputs and selects to use the available width, and moves animation controls to one column. The settings page clips horizontal overflow at its own boundary. These changes are scoped below 720px, matching the ADR and the existing responsive layout composable, so tablet and desktop styles remain in force above that point. No config schema or raw TOML-only option was added.

Coverage now checks the mobile section chooser and its seven existing destinations, tab routing, retention of existing fields, save error feedback after a failed autosave, and the desktop tablist at the breakpoint’s desktop side. The error test makes the store’s save method fail and confirms the inline error remains visible, exercising the existing error behavior through the mobile UI.

## Approaches tried

I first added the Settings chooser while continuing to render the existing panels, then added narrow-only wrapping and sizing rules. I considered building mobile-specific copies of individual forms, but using the existing tab IDs, panels, schema fields, and store avoids divergent behavior and keeps deep links and save semantics intact. I also kept General section links as-is; they already wrap and address URL-backed sections, so reworking them was unnecessary for this slice.

The first scoped gate exposed an assumption in the shared responsive hook: multiple existing Settings tests provide lightweight `matchMedia` objects without the modern change-event methods. I updated the hook to fall back to window resize handling when those methods are absent and made cleanup safe for those test doubles. This also accommodates older WebViews while leaving browsers with `MediaQueryList` events on the preferred path.

## Challenges and blockers

The initial test run failed because the responsive hook assumed every `matchMedia` result implemented `addEventListener` and `removeEventListener`. Once the hook handled the partial interface, all pre-existing Settings mounts passed. A later run caught an over-specific assertion in the new test that expected one cleanup call; the view and nested Settings components each use the shared hook, so cleanup may be called several times. I changed the assertion to verify cleanup occurs without assuming a single consumer.

A formatter check then identified formatting changes, which I applied with `bun run fmt`. The required scoped `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` subsequently passed: formatting, lint, build, changed-path tests on the remote validation runner, browser gate, rendered contrast audit, and local UI smoke all completed successfully. The local build and browser audit waited for RepoOS’s pressure and Playwright slot queues, then finished without failure.

## Key learnings

For a view that participates in responsive composition, tests may supply incomplete browser API doubles even when production browsers expose the full interface. Shared composables should be resilient at the API boundary and retain a fallback path instead of forcing every consumer to mock a full browser object. Also, a separate mobile navigation does not require a separate settings data model: reusing route state and panels preserves both behavior and URL compatibility while still allowing a purpose-built layout.
